title: Objects — The World Around You
description: Twelve things you can point at right now — a glass of water, the door, your phone — heard in Cairo Arabic and seen until the sound and the thing are one. No reading, no speaking yet.
approach: GPA Phase 1 — Here & Now. Receptive only: listen, look, tap. No production, no grammar meta-language.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 correct on the final listen-and-tap quiz
can_do: Recognise twelve everyday objects by sound and picture
Match a spoken Egyptian word to the thing it names

culture.title: The glass of tea is where the language starts
culture.note: Walk into any Egyptian home, shop or office and before anything else you will be asked what you drink. Tea (شاي) is the default — black, strong, and sweet unless you say otherwise — and Turkish-style coffee (قهوة) comes in a small cup, ordered by its sugar level. Say yes the second time you are asked, not the first: the first offer is the ritual, the second is the invitation. Learning these two words before anything else is not an accident; they are the first words a host will say to you.

phrases.english: What will you drink? Tea or coffee?

vocabulary.teaching_note: Universal and unambiguous. The Egyptian word is مية (mayya), with a doubled y — not the MSA ماء, and not the Gulf ماي. You will hear it a hundred times a day in summer.
vocabulary.image_scene: Close-up of a clear glass of cold water on a table, condensation on the glass, a plastic water bottle beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone pouring or asking for water; مية said while the glass or bottle is on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Culturally central and the first meeting with the Egyptian ق: it is written ق but said as a catch in the throat, ʾahwa. Learners who say qahwa sound like a newsreader. The same word means the neighbourhood café (الأهوة).
vocabulary.image_scene: A small white Turkish-coffee cup on a saucer with thick dark coffee, a long-handled brass kanaka pot behind it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Coffee being made in a kanaka or ordered at a café; the word said as the cup arrives.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The national drink, served in a glass, black and sweet. The same word across the Arab world, so it is a free win — and the first ش sound.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small glass of dark red-brown tea on a metal tray, a sugar bowl beside it, a sprig of mint on top.
vocabulary.video_hint: A glass of tea being poured or offered; the host asking 'tea or coffee?'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Egyptians call bread عيش — literally 'life'. The MSA and Levantine خبز will be understood but marks you as a foreigner at once. Introduces the ع sound at the start of a word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A stack of round puffed Egyptian baladi flatbreads on a wooden board, one torn open to show the pocket.
vocabulary.video_hint: Baladi bread on the table, at the bakery window or being torn to scoop fuul; cooking channels name it constantly.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Furniture is ideal early vocabulary — stable, pointable, unambiguous. Same word everywhere in Arabic.
vocabulary.image_scene: A simple wooden chair with a cane seat against a plain light wall, nothing else in frame.
vocabulary.video_hint: A chair being pointed at, pulled up or sat on in a home tour or a café scene.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Short, phonetically simple, and it carries the long aa the learner will meet again in كتاب. Egyptians knock and call يا باب? — not literally, but the word is everywhere.
vocabulary.image_scene: A wooden apartment door slightly ajar with warm light coming through the gap, a brass knocker on it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone at, opening or knocking on a door; flat-tour clips saying الباب.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Very high frequency; it returns in dozens of later phrases (بيتي، بيتك، بيتنا). Note the Egyptian vowel: beet, a long ee, not bayt. That ee sound is the most audible mark of a Cairo accent.
vocabulary.image_scene: Exterior of a Cairo apartment building in warm light, balconies with washing lines and potted plants, a small shop at street level.
vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger arriving home or showing the building from outside; بيت/بيتنا in the narration.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The everyday Egyptian word for a car is عربية, not سيارة (which is what the sign on a car-hire office says). Confusingly the same word also means 'Arabic' as an adjective — context always tells you which. Doubled يّ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A white saloon car parked under a tree on a quiet Cairo side street, seen from the side.
vocabulary.video_hint: Getting into or talking about a car; driving vlogs and traffic complaints are full of العربية.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first ج of the course, and in Cairo ج is a hard g: shagara, never shajara. Say it the Cairo way from day one — it is the sound Egyptians notice first in a foreigner. Cairo's streets are lined with ficus and palms, so trees are pointable.
vocabulary.image_scene: A tall date palm beside a leafy ficus tree on a Cairo street corner, clear blue sky.
vocabulary.video_hint: A palm or garden tree shown while named; garden and Nile-side vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A borrowed word, so nearly free. Egyptians say موبايل for the phone in their hand and تليفون for a call or a landline; both are accepted. Gulf جوال will not be understood in Cairo.
vocabulary.image_scene: A smartphone lying face-up on a café table, screen lit, next to a glass of tea.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone holding up, charging or looking for their phone; موبايل is the word to listen for.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Classic object-lesson word; long aa vowel, and the ك–ت–ب root the learner will meet again in 'write' and 'office'. Same word in every dialect.
vocabulary.image_scene: A closed hardback book on a desk, plain cover, a pen resting on top.

example.english: The book is on the chair

vocabulary.video_hint: A book being held or shown; study vlogs, bookshop tours, children's read-alongs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Everyday and pocket-sized. Introduces the ح sound at the end of a word, where it is easiest to hear. Egyptians say muftaaḥ with u in the first syllable.
vocabulary.image_scene: A single metal key on a keyring against a plain background.

example.english: The key is in the car

vocabulary.video_hint: Keys being picked up or searched for on the way out; 'المفتاح فين؟'.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.english: The water is on the chair

sound_spotlight.explanation: In Cairo ج is a hard g as in 'go', never the j of MSA or the Levant. It is the single most recognisable Egyptian sound, and it is introduced through the first word that has it.

Written ق, but in everyday Cairo speech it is a catch in the throat, like the gap in 'uh-oh'. Learners must learn to read ق and hear ʾ. A handful of learned words keep the q (القرآن، القاهرة) — those come later.
A squeezed sound from deep in the throat, unlike anything in English. Heard passively here in two of the most useful words; production practice starts in Lesson 3.
Where other dialects say bayt, Cairo says beet — a long, pure ee. Hearing it in two words side by side lets the pattern register before it is ever explained.

lesson_sequence.detail: A warm Cairo street scene — balconies, a palm, a tea tray. One line of English: you will start recognising twelve Egyptian words. Tap يلا to begin.
Each of the 12 words on its own full-screen card: illustration, native Cairo audio auto-plays, Arabic large, no English yet. Tap to replay as often as you like.
The same 12 cards, faster, audio auto-plays, English label now shown small and grey underneath.
Audio only; four images in a grid; tap the one you heard. Words 1–6. Distractors come from this lesson.
Random order, audio only. Score screen shows the missed words with image and audio to replay.
Words-learned counter rolls up to 12. Nudge: look around you today and find these things.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Look around you right now. Can you spot any of the twelve things from this lesson? Say the Egyptian word in your head.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Observation only, no speaking required. Activates all 12 words.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Every time you make or drink شاي or مية over the next few days, say the word once out loud.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification the next morning (optional). Two of the highest-frequency words, both in every kitchen.

real_world_prompts.prompt: If you have a tutor session coming up, tell them: 'I just learned these twelve words — can you point at them and say them?'
real_world_prompts.context: The ideal first tutor interaction: the GPA here-and-now game. Receptive reinforcement only.

video_needs.scene: A host or vlogger naming objects while they are on screen: tea poured into a glass, baladi bread on the table, keys and phone picked up on the way to the car.
